What is set out on the page devoted to the historical notes on the territory, important as it is, suggests that perhaps the essence of this walk also lies elsewhere: in folk culture, in encounters, in the stories that came to life in the lands touched by this Way, with the web of interrelations they have woven among themselves over time.

The Salt Roads were a unique and decisive phenomenon for the economic, social and cultural development of the whole region between the Taro and the Scrivia (and beyond: there are others too, running from western Liguria towards Piedmont).

They perfectly express the tangle of dynamics produced by the tension between those who travel and those who stay, that is, between constant transit and settled life. They therefore made a fundamental contribution to building the collective identity of the people who lived in these places. The Antica Via del Cifalco, having been travelled first and foremost for trade, can rightfully be regarded as one of the Salt Roads, and indeed as one of the most important.

Salt

Salt is an ingredient of such importance in the European and global economy that, without it, the world as we know it today simply would not exist. Had salt not been traded, it would not have been possible to preserve food; there would be no cured meats, cheeses, herrings, salt cod and many other foods that have allowed humankind to get by. Agriculture, too, would not have gone beyond certain limits since, without the food waste discarded by people (e.g. whey), it would have been harder to feed livestock and hence also to have enough dung for manuring. In short, without salt humanity could not have completed that “agricultural revolution” which freed it from the level of hunter-gatherers. In even more immediate terms, most of the foods we eat every day would be inedible without salt, and many of its other uses (e.g. spreading it after a frost) would be denied to us.

The salt trade between Genoa and the Po plain probably goes back to prehistoric times. In fact, for a long time the turnover of this trade remained modest, chiefly because of the considerable cost of carrying goods by pack mule over rugged ridges.

And yet, from the 14th century onwards, control of the salt pans became a geopolitical matter. Venice controlled the output of the salt pans in the eastern Mediterranean (Tripoli, Cyprus, Malta, Turkey, Apulia, Split, Zadar and some stretches of Greece), opposed by Genoa in the western Mediterranean (Sicily, Hières, Cagliari and Ibiza). Genoa, moreover, gradually widened its sphere of influence in this field, as it oversaw not only production but also transport, particularly towards Emilia, Piedmont and France.

And so, together with the religious work of the Benedictines of the abbey of San Colombano and of the network of other monasteries built under its impetus, from the 16th century the salt trade contributed to the spread of a dense web of roads and paths, reflecting a complex system of economic and political relations.

The Via Patranica

It is no coincidence that the route unanimously regarded as the first and foremost Salt Road is the so-called “Via Patranica”. It takes its name from the Benedictine abbey that stood between Montebruno and Torriglia in Val Trebbia and that called that portion of territory “Patrania”. The place name is said to derive from the landholdings that came from the “patres”, the “fathers”, and that from at least the 3rd century AD were managed under the system of “comunalie”, that is, communally. It seems that the abbey was founded by the Lombards between the 7th and 8th centuries, and the last mention of it in an official document dates from 1266.

According to some, the abbey had two seats, one in Torriglia and one in Montebruno. However, every trace of it has now been completely lost, including knowledge of the exact place where it stood. In any case, for a long time the Salt Roads were referred to as the “patraniche”, that is, the ones which, with all their variants, passed through the territory of Patrania.

As proof of how fluid Apennine routes were over the centuries, there was, more precisely, a “Patranic route” that followed a basic outline, with some alternatives and several junction points depending on the seaside town one set out from. The same can, after all, be said of the Strada del Cifalco. Other routes crossing it in various ways would then gradually have been added to this outline, until a genuine network of paths took shape.

The likely junction for joining this “Patranic route” which, from Chiavari, cut across the territory between Torriglia and Montebruno, was probably on the slopes of Monte Lavagnola, above the Passo della Scoffera, which separates Val Trebbia from Val Fontanabuona. Indeed, even those who walked the Via del Cifalco intending to go down to Genoa headed precisely in this direction once they reached Barbagelata. At any rate, one can say that the Strada Patranica sums up well the mixed origin – religious and economic – of Apennine roads over the centuries, as well as the vagueness of all the detours and variants into which these routes branched.

The “other” Salt Roads

It also follows, however, that this route, however important historically and perhaps even the first of all, was not the only Salt Road. On the Apennines between the Taro and the Scrivia there are seven passes that marked as many crucial lines of communication. From east to west, they are: the Passo della Cisa; the Passo del Brattello; the Passo delle Cento Croci; the Passo del Bocco; the Valico della Forcella; the Passo della Scoglina; and the Passo della Scoffera. Each of them is so rich in History (and stories) as to deserve a treatment of its own.

The one of most interest here is the Passo della Scoglina, since the Strada del Cifalco passes over it on the route proposed here. This is somewhat paradoxical given that, historically, it gained importance more recently than the others: it is in fact likely that many caravans crossed the watershed between the “continental” and the “maritime” Apennines by way of the smaller passes of Acquapendente and Possarelli, only later passing by the present-day Scoglina pass, very close to them. The very name “Scoglina” appears to be a relatively recent, 19th-century attribution to what in the past was known instead as the Passo della Volta.

It goes without saying that there were in fact hundreds of roads, and they went well beyond the crossings of these seven main passes. Besides, even in specialist works there is no full agreement on which were the main Salt Roads and exactly where they ran – see “The uncertain origins of the Antica Via del Cifalco”, on this website.

In the “Other walks” section there is information on whether many of these routes can be walked today.

By mule

The Strada del Cifalco, as an ancient trade route, was first and foremost travelled by mules and muleteers. Picturing it today seems incredible: the ridge path that now appears so silent to our senses hosted an unceasing passage of caravans, to the point that in many places people had to stop to let traffic flow in both directions!

A muleteer generally owned four or five mules, but could also travel with hundreds of animals. The muleteers of the time could be recognised from afar by the heavy cloak (“ferraiolo”) they wrapped themselves in during the winter, from which only one hand emerged, holding the whip. To ensure their safety, several muleteers often “joined forces” to make the crossings together: indeed, attack by brigands was a constant risk, to which was added the danger of wolves for the animals, especially in summer when people slept out in the open.

But the hardest season was undoubtedly winter. An old proverb of Val Trebbia and Val d’Aveto runs: “Whoever wants to taste the torments of hell should be a blacksmith in summer and a muleteer in winter”.

Falling into the water while fording a stream could mean freezing for both muleteer and mules. This is one of the reasons why the Antica Via del Cifalco established itself as a much-used mule track: being a ridge route, it keeps stream crossings to a minimum. In practice, along the whole route the only watercourse to cross was the Lavagna torrent; and that only for those coming from the Tigullio, since those climbing up from Genoa avoided even that by going over the Passo della Scoffera and Monte Lavagnola, then climbing to Barbagelata. From Ponte Organasco onwards, as far as Bobbio and then the plain, the river to cross was the Trebbia, often turbulent in winter; but there, probably since Roman times, stood a convenient bridge, the very one that gives the village its name and that for centuries was the only way to cross the river safely within a radius of tens of kilometres. In short, compared with other Salt Roads, only in a few cases did the muleteers of the Via del Cifalco have to resort to “passiere” (tall, shaped stones placed a stride apart, which could be walked on) and “sgarampi” (stilts for wading straight across the watercourse). On the other hand, like the Via dell’Antola (known to hikers today as the “Via del Sale” or “Via del Mare”), this too was a disadvantageous option in winter, since it lay at altitude and was therefore very exposed to the fury of the elements, in particular wind and snow. Back then, winters were another matter altogether.

The muleteer’s toil could never have paid off without the help of his animal, the indestructible mule. The offspring of a mare and a donkey, it has the sturdiness and speed of the one and the endurance and adaptability of the other. It can carry loads of up to 100 kg for many hours, feeding only on oats and barley; moreover, it can tread rugged paths barely 30 cm wide, albeit with its proverbial fondness for the edge of the precipice. Although the ancient Romans knew mules well, it is likely that until well into the Middle Ages the Strada del Cifalco was travelled more by donkeys than by mules, which prevailed thanks to their greater strength only at a later stage. Some even claim that the Far West was actually settled on muleback rather than on horseback, despite what film imagery served up to us throughout the 20th century.

The mule, however, required a great deal of care. At the end of each day’s journey, to prevent theft during the night, the goods had to be unloaded and stored in depots sometimes set up on the spot (as on the grasslands of M. Dego), if there were no inns or taverns. Then the animals had to be cleaned, groomed and fed. The next morning, bridles, packsaddle and load had to be fitted again.

Incidentally, transport techniques did not evolve much over time, remaining essentially the same for 3000 years, particularly in their heyday between the Late Middle Ages and the 20th century, when the two wars and the building of asphalt roads along the valley floors marked the end of this phenomenon and of the way of life bound up with it.

Rural civilisation on the Salt Roads and their inhabitants

The enormous importance the Salt Roads took on from the 16th century produced significant physical and social mobility. This, in turn, fostered the emergence of a culture founded on the epic of transport by mule, which naturally also included those who – directly or indirectly – gravitated around that activity.

The villages along the Roads or nearby became places of rest and shelter for the caravans; they offered work, entertainment and evenings spent listening to tales of exploits, fortunes, dramas and comic episodes. Several villages around the Antica Via del Cifalco that today are abandoned, if not actually derelict or in ruins, at certain times came to host 10 or 15 taverns! Consider that in Fontanigorda alone there were still as many as six in business after the Second World War: thinking about it today, it seems like science fiction.

This is why it would actually be more accurate to refer to these roads as “ancient mule tracks”. First of all, salt was not the only product carried by the traders who shuttled between the plain and the sea. Moreover, these muleteers were in good company: gendarmes, vagrants, beggars, musicians, brigands, tumblers and... “orsanti”!

The latter were wanderers who travelled with their trained animals (mostly bears, but also monkeys and sometimes even dromedaries!). They made them perform to entertain an impromptu audience: they could make the animals dance, jump and thrash about. The highlight was the fight between the tamer and the beast; a piece of play-acting – whoever invented wrestling must have taken inspiration from them – but the unpredictability of the bear made this kind of show dangerous in itself, and therefore thrilling for the audience. The act invariably ended with the animal on the ground, defeated as if dead, dragged off the stage to the applause of the spectators.

In fact, the orsanti lived on offerings and charity; but all of them, rebelling against the prospect of a life of hardship and poverty, dreamed of making their fortune by setting off on adventure. The trade took hold in Cavignaga, in the upper Val di Taro (Parma), but spread like wildfire along all the ridges of the Apennines between the Taro and the Scrivia. It often became a family tradition handed down through the generations. Especially from the 10th century onwards, a slice of merriment, spontaneous life and longing for freedom swept through the Apennines for several centuries; this is another reason why we hope that the collection of the Museo degli Orsanti, first housed in Compiano, then in Vigoleno and now closed, will soon find a new home.

This motley crowd of assorted characters, who brushed past one another, met, interacted, laughed, quarrelled and perhaps even killed one another, lived on the margins of the great political events. Yet they gave rise to a folk culture and literature – mostly oral – of which little remains to us, but which, until the advent of industrialisation and the two wars, brightened the lives of the people of this stretch of the Apennines.

That said, everyday life on these mountains over the centuries should not be idealised. People lived in difficult conditions, doing hard work in rugged and also rather unsafe areas. The tendency towards a political and jurisdictional “leopard-spot” patchwork, a constant feature of these mountains up to the two wars, carried its consequences to the extreme after the abolition of the Imperial Ligurian Fiefs. The many bandits who, for better or worse, had had to restrain themselves so as not to disturb the established order serving the desiderata of the lords they depended on, and who shielded them from the municipal authorities, began to run riot unchecked under Napoleon’s rule. To them was added the grey zone of shepherds, woodcutters and charcoal burners who lived outside the villages and who, as soon as the chance arose, did not hesitate to rob, hold up and often even murder hapless travellers, then making the bodies disappear with great nonchalance into the fire or into impenetrable crevices. All the more so once the petty lords and their henchmen who patrolled the territory were gone, hardly anyone took the trouble to investigate all these mysterious disappearances.

The settlements

While referring to the section “The stages of the Via del Cifalco through history, nature and culture” for the particular features of each individual village, it can already be said that the settlements around the Strada del Cifalco share some common traits, both on the Trebbia side and on the Aveto side. These are not only architectural elements, but also the social structures of the times when life pulsed here, or at least before the spectre of depopulation descended on these mountains.

The model of the “stone house” with exposed stonework, typical of the Genoese Apennines, comes in a great many variants. Ponte Organasco and Cerignale are two almost unsurpassable examples of the genre. Windows are few and narrow, as protection against the winter frosts; exposed wooden beams are all the rage among the old ceilings; and roofs were built with slabs of slate (“ciappe”, in the local speech). Today, sadly, even the few period houses that have been restored have the ordinary red-tiled roofs we are used to; just you try finding a builder who can still make a roof “a ciappe”!

A typical place for socialising was the cowshed: the youngest members of large families made themselves beds in the hay to sleep in. There, wayfarers, beggars or friends from neighbouring valleys who had come for festivals or funerals, or who were stranded by bad weather, were also put up, in keeping with a culture of hospitality and respect for the traveller that is still deeply rooted today.

The villages of the area do not seem to have been designed to meet defensive needs. There are almost never walls, bridges linking the houses (here Brignole is a small exception) or covered passageways. This is further proof that History, with its power struggles over resources and strategic areas, spent more time avoiding these lands than lingering in them. In the villages, the prevailing form tends to be elongated along a main route, a sign of transit rather than of stopping. Fontanigorda, for example.

The settlements are striking for their compactness: the houses huddle against one another and are often separated by a single wall. Seen from the summits and slopes of the mountains, they convey an idea of unity and protection, as if barricaded against a wild and hostile nature. This is particularly so at Orezzoli di qua and Orezzoli di là.

This also meant a structural sharing of spaces and rhythms of daily life for the people who lived there. The impression of togetherness suggested by their “urban” layout, rather spontaneous as it is, also brings another consequence with it: the sharp break between town and countryside. Just outside the village the fields began and, immediately after, the woods. Our eyes are no longer used to this visual break: raising our heads from the historic centres of our cities, or even just our small towns or villages, we almost never glimpse the countryside, but most of the time only an expanse of hideous concrete silhouettes. In this respect, the villages around the Trebbia-Aveto ridge such as Ottone Soprano, Toveraia and Brignole, for all their silent abandonment, invite us to reflect. In the past there was a synergy between living together and living off the land: each nourished the other and gave substance to its completion. Today, for entire generations no longer able to hold a hoe or tell a bee from a wasp, all that remains is to ask ourselves about the need for, and the importance of, keeping alive an umbilical cord between these two dimensions.

Slate

We mentioned roofs “a ciappe”. These were slabs of a material that for centuries was an irreplaceable resource: slate.

It was much more than a mere activity: it has played a decisive role in the economic, social and hence also landscape history of the area since the 12th century. For our walk, too, it carries symbolic importance: in a way, it links cultural aspects of the “maritime” Apennines, where it was quarried and worked, with others of the “continental” Apennines, where it could be admired on the roofs of the houses.

It is a sedimentary rock with the priceless property of being splittable into thin slabs without crumbling. Each bed of slate, which for centuries men had to dig out with their bare hands beneath the roots of the chestnut trees of Val Fontanabuona, was found inside other layers of rock. Many of the paths by which every corner of that valley can be reached today were built precisely to allow quarrying and transport. In the 19th century, output reached about 10,000 tonnes of slate a year in Val Fontanabuona alone and in a few other small basins in the hinterland of the Ligurian Levante.

Climbing up to the Passo dei Casetti, the abandoned quarries are striking and spectacular. The earliest documents confirming the quarrying of slate for commercial purposes date from the 12th century and refer precisely to these slopes.

Comuni, “comunalie” and “Comunelli”

The Strada del Cifalco, on the route proposed here, winds through two Regions (Emilia-Romagna and Liguria) and no fewer than 17 Comuni: Cerignale and Ottone in the province of Piacenza; Rovegno, Rezzoaglio, Fontanigorda, Montebruno, Lorsica, Neirone, Moconesi, Tribogna, Uscio, Avegno, Recco, Rapallo, Camogli, Santa Margherita and Portofino in the province of Genoa. Note that the Way mostly runs along the boundary line between many of these municipalities.

Add to this that not only the fields, but also the woods and pastures were managed under the age-old system of “comunalie”. They therefore belonged to the whole village.

Believe it or not, this institution has in fact survived intact to this day through the creation of the “Comunelli”, consortium bodies that exercise public or quasi-public powers over mountain resources, namely hunting, grazing, forestry and mushroom picking. Some are truly ancient: this is the case, for example, of Alpepiana, which itself already appears in a royal document of Liutprand dated AD 714 and was an important Lombard administrative centre.

The existence of these Comunelli and the ways they manage their prerogatives often stir controversy. They are, in fact, often inspired by rules that are still medieval – or older – and, while in practice taking the exercise of these tasks away from the Comuni, they have no real constitutional basis. And so, not content with passing through the territory of 17 Comuni, the Antica Via del Cifalco also crosses a large number of Comunelli, each subject to its own rules, customs and traditions. This, too, expresses the cross-border nature of the walk and, at the same time, the extraordinary diversity of situations found in these lands.
